title: Junior competitions and costs
summary: From club shoots to international events in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting: the Junior category from 2027, the rules young shooters follow, and the costs to plan for.

body.html: A good place for a child’s first competitions is your own club: club shoots are short, friendly and low in pressure. Next come regional and national events and, with experience, international FITASC competitions in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting.

FITASC uses a new table of categories from 1 January 2027. Under it, boys and girls are Juniors from 1 January of the year they turn 13 until the end of the year they turn 20. For 2027 that means born in 2007–2014; only the year of birth counts. A junior’s score counts twice: in the Junior category and in the open ranking, where everyone competes together.

All six FITASC categories are Junior (13–20), Lady (from 13), Men (21–55), Senior (56–65), Veteran (66–72) and Master (from 73), counted by year of birth, not by birthday. These are international rules: national and club events may use their own categories and age limits, so read the programme. More: Categories, classes and shoot-offs.

A FITASC team usually has three shooters; the Men team in Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ has four. A shooter picked for a team of another category must also enter that category individually: a junior girl in the Lady team, for example, also enters Lady.

Juniors follow the same rules as adults: safety, dress, the ban on coaching, and the rules for guns and cartridges. The gun rules: a smooth-bore shotgun no larger than 12 gauge, with barrels at least 66 cm (26 in) long; pump-action guns are not allowed. Gauge is the width of the barrel, and a higher number means a narrower barrel, so a 20-gauge gun (narrower, usually lighter) is allowed. A cartridge may hold at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated).

During the competition nobody may coach a shooter, and that includes parents. If the referee sees coaching, the shooter gets a yellow card and the adviser is sent out of the shooting area. How to support without pressure: Juniors and parents: support without pressure.

Now the costs, in general terms. Regular spending goes on targets and cartridges, usually the biggest item, plus lessons with a coach. One-off spending goes on kit: a gun or its hire, protection, a vest and shoes. Each year there is club membership, the federation’s sports licence and insurance. Competitions add entry fees, travel and accommodation.

Plan a budget for the season and add costs step by step. Ask the club about junior discounts, club guns and second-hand kit; some clubs and federations run support programmes for juniors. What the sport costs: What the budget is made of; a plan for the first year: A first-year plan.

key_points.html: Junior in the FITASC table from 2027: from 1 January of the year they turn 13 until the end of the year they turn 20.
Juniors follow the adult rules; a 20-gauge gun is allowed.
No advice from the side during the round: it can cost the young shooter a yellow card.
The main costs are targets and cartridges; plan a season budget.

did_you_know.html: For FITASC categories only the year of birth matters: a shooter born on 31 December moves to the next category on 1 January, just like one born in January.

quiz.q: Who is in the Junior category in the FITASC table from 2027?

options.text: Everyone up to the year they turn 25
From the year they turn 13 to the year they turn 20
Only boys, from the year they turn 12 to 16

quiz.explain: Junior runs from 1 January of the year a shooter turns 13 to 31 December of the year they turn 20, for girls and boys.

quiz.q: Does a junior take part in the open ranking?

options.text: No, only in the Junior ranking
Only if they win the Junior ranking
Yes, together with the Junior ranking

quiz.explain: One score counts in both the open ranking and the category ranking.

quiz.q: What is usually the largest regular cost?
quiz.explain: Targets and cartridges are used at each session, so budget for them first.
